column2: Why text needs to be numbered
column5:
Text must be transformed into numbers before LLM.
A chunk of text is a “token” and can be a character, subword, or full word.
Embeddings are dense representations of tokens.
Tokenization and embeddings are learned from data, and there are many ways to create these schemes.

Text can be split into words via spaces, although this is not done in real tokenization.
Encoder and decoder functions are simple look-up tables.
Tokenization (encoding text using integers) is conceptually straightforward.

Encoders and decoders are created using dictionary comprehension and functions.
The “context” of a token is its neighbors (before and possibly after); “context window” is the number of neighbors.
“One-hot encoding” is a sparse tokenization, with one row per token and one column per vocab item.

Real text from the web is easy to import but a pain to clean…
Creating a tokenizing scheme is tricky and involves many choices with few clear optimal decisions.
Encoders and decoders are easy to create and use.

Randomly generated tokens are usually nonsensical.
There is a mathematical relationship between word length and frequency (more on this later!), which has implications for LLM performance.
Tokenizers need special characters to deal with unknown tokens.

column2: CodeChallenge: Math with tokens and embeddings

Cosine similarity is one of the most commonly used measures of a relationship between two variables when working with embeddings and LLMs.
Cosine similarity is related to correlation: Both variance-normalize; Pearson additionally mean-centers.
Use the correlation to quantify a linear relationship in data that have different scales or mean offsets.
But when the variables are in the same scale and offsets are meaningful, use cosine similarity. This is often the case in LLM investigations.
When learning a new technical topic, try to code the math yourself; in applications, use established libraries if available and if it’s easier.

Language models use position embeddings to focus on tokens from various locations (“time points”) in the token sequence.

Terms and datatypes in math and computers
column5:
Some important terms in linear algebra and python include scalar, vector, matrix, and tensor.
There are "types" of numbers and variables, which can have different meanings in math vs. coding.

"Transpose" is an operation in linear algebra that involves swapping rows and columns in a vector or matrix.
It's used a lot in linear algebra and deep learning, as you'll see in the next several videos.

Linear weighted combinations are simple yet foundational in deep learning (and countless other applications!).
Non-zero means do not necessarily bias the results.
Simulating data and examining distributions can be very insightful when learning math.

There are several notations of the dot product.
“Dot product” is just a fancy term for linear weighted combination.
Libraries have built-in functions to calculate the dot product.
PyTorch is more sensitive to datatypes than is numpy (a common source of errors!).

Matrix multiplication is valid only when “inner” matrix dimensions match.
Matrix multiplication is just an organized collection of dot products.
There are multiple ways to calculate matrix multiplication in numpy and pytorch.
PyTorch functions can be sensitive to datatype.

"Softmax" is a mathematical operation used in deep learning to transform a set of numbers (often called "logits") into probabilities.
Softmax is a nonlinear transformation. Inputs can be negative, but all outputs are positive.
Language models use softmax to help select tokens (subwords).

The logarithm is a nonlinear transformation of positive-valued numbers.
It is often used in machine-learning and optimization to "stretch out" small numbers such as p-values.

Entropy is a mathematical measures of the "surprise" or unexpectedness of a system. It can be used as a measure of nonlinear variability.
In deep learning, entropy and cross-entropy are used as error signals to train language models to select words that are consistent with human text.

Min and max refer to the smallest (most negative) and largest values in a vector or matrix.
The "arg" prefix refers to the index in the matrix where the extreme value was observed.

The mean is the average of a collection of numbers (sum divided by count). It is used as a measure of the most typical or representative number.
Variance is the amount of dispersion in the data. Larger variance means the data values are more spread out around the mean.

Repeatedly taking data from a population will give different results. This is called "sampling variability."
Sampling variability is a foundation of statistics, and is used in language modeling to probabilistically select from among the most likely next tokens.

The t-test is a statistical evaluation that indicates whether the average of one group is different from the average of another group.
The t-test has countless applications; in this course, we'll use the t-test when evaluating model performance and investigating circuits and mechanisms in attention layers.

A derivative describes how a function changes. There are analytic (pure math) techniques for finding the derivative of a function, but you can also approximate it by calculating differences between neighboring points of a function.
Among other uses, derivatives are used to find the minimum values of a function.
Derivatives are central to training a language model: Represent the model's error as a loss function, calculate its derivative, and then use the derivative to find the model parameters that minimize the error.

Because the derivative indicates whether a function is increasing or decreasing, it can be used to point towards function minima.
In deep learning including large language models, the functions and their derivatives are simple, but have so many variables that they cannot be fully calculated analytically. Therefore, estimation methods like gradient descent are used to find minima.
There are some potentially difficult issues like local minima and vanishing gradients; modern techniques have some ways of avoiding these kinds of issues to help obtain good models.

This video introduces two differentiation techniques for multiplied (product rule) and compound (chain rule) functions. Pytorch handles the implementational details of differentiation, but understanding more about derivatives will help you understand backprop.

Gradient descent is the core algorithm that powers deep learning, by iteratively finding weights (parameters) that allow the model to learn structure in text data to classify and generate new text.
A "gradient" is another word for the derivative, and thus, gradient descent simply involves calculating the local derivative of the loss function, and nudging the weights in the direction that decreases the loss.
There are some modern techniques to help gradient descent perform well in large models, but the core method hasn't really changed in decades.

The optimization goal of training deep learning models is to find the *global* minimum of the error function, but gradient descent can get caught in *local* minima.
Although this can be problematic in relatively small models, large network models rarely suffer from local minima, in part because there are so few (most apparent local minima are actually saddle points, where the function can go down a different direction).
Modern optimizers such as Adam can adaptively navigate other potential issues such as vanishing gradients.

Gradient descent in a 1D (single-variable) function provides a great visual intuition for how and why gradient decent works.
This demo also reveals why gradient descent is not guaranteed to provide the global optimal solution (although it will be a good approximation given some assumptions).

This videos shows how gradient descent is extended from 1D (single-variable function) to 2D (two-variable function). The principles and the math are the same, but the implementation and possibile outcomes are slightly more complicated.
